{{italic title}}
'''''Linear Operators''''' is a three-volume textbook on the theory of [[linear operators]], written by [[Nelson Dunford]] and [[Jacob T. Schwartz]]. The three volumes are (I) ''General Theory''; (II) ''Spectral Theory, Self Adjoint Operators in Hilbert Space''; and (III) ''Spectral Operators''. The first volume was published in 1958, the second in 1963, and the third in 1971. All three volumes were reprinted by [[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] in 1988. Canonically cited as '''Dunford and Schwartz''',<ref name=MacTutor/> the textbook has been referred to as "the definitive work" on linear operators.<ref name=DavisSchonberg/>{{rp|2}}

The work began as a written set of solutions to the problems for Dunford's graduate course in linear operators at [[Yale University|Yale]].<ref name=Rota>{{cite book |last=Rota |first=Gian-Carlo |title=Indiscrete Thoughts |publisher=Birkhauser |date=1997 }}</ref>{{rp|30}}<ref name=MacTutor>{{MacTutor |title=Jacob T Schwartz |id=Schwartz_Jacob |date=April 2009 }}</ref> Schwartz, a prodigy, had taken his undergraduate degree at Yale in 1948, age 18. In 1949 he began his graduate studies and enrolled in his course. Dunford recognised Schwartz's intelligence and they began a long collaboration, with Dunford acting as Schwartz's advisor for his dissertation ''Linear Elliptic Differential Operators''.<ref name=MacTutor/><ref name=Rota/>{{rp|30}} One fruit of their collaboration was the [[Dunford-Schwartz theorem]].<ref name=memoir/>{{rp|4}} The work was originally intended to be a short introduction to [[functional analysis]] (the original material comprising what was published as Chapters 2, 4, 7 and part of 10 in Volume I) but the material ballooned.<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|32}} The work enjoyed funding from the [[Office of Naval Research]] and a popular joke at the time was that every nuclear submarine had a copy.<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|30}} [[William G. Bade]] and [[Robert G. Bartle]] were brought on as research assistants.<ref>{{cite journal |first=H. G. |last=Dales |title=William George Bade 1924–2012 |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=45 |date=2013 |pages=875–888 |doi=10.1112/blms/bdt037 }}</ref> Dunford retired shortly after finishing the final volume.<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|30}} Schwartz, however, went on to write similarly pathbreaking books in various other areas of mathematics.<ref name=MacTutor/>{{efn|To give some impression of Schwartz's energies: in the three-year period between the publication of the second and third volumes of ''Linear Operators'', Schwartz published a book on [[W*-algebras]] (1967), one on [[Lie algebras]] (1968), and one on [[nonlinear functional analysis]] (1969).<ref name=MacTutor/>}}

The book met with acclaim when published. It won the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] in 1981, awarded by the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name=DavisSchonberg>{{cite book |editor1-last=Davis |editor1-first=Martin |editor2-last=Schonberg |editor2-first=Edmond |title=From Linear Operators to Computational Biology: Essays in Memory of Jacob T. Schwartz |publisher=Springer |date=2013 }}</ref>{{rp|2}} In the citation for this prize, the committee observed "This monumental work of 2,592 pages must be the most comprehensive of its kind in mathematics ... A whole generation of analysts has been trained from it."<ref name=DunfordObit>{{cite journal |title=Nelson Dunford, 1906-1986 |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |page=287 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/198702/198702FullIssue.pdf?adat=February%201987&trk=&cat=none&type=.pdf#page=65 |volume=34 |date=February 1987 |issue=2 }}</ref> [[Peter Lax]] remarked that it "contained everything known, and many things not yet known, on linear functional analysis."<ref name=memoir/>{{rp|6}} [[Béla Szőkefalvi-Nagy]] wrote in a review of the first volume: "the authors have created an extraordinarily important and valuable work that is distinguished in particular by its monumental completeness, clear organization, and attractive exposition".<ref name=memoir/>{{rp|6}} [[Gian-Carlo Rota]], who was involved in checking the exercises, wrote that "the contrast between the uncompromising abstraction of the text and the incredible variety of the concrete examples in the exercises is immensely beneficial to any student learning [[mathematical analysis]]."<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|33}}

Every chapter of the book ends with a section entitled "Notes and Remarks", giving historical background on the topic and informal discussion of related topics. The book contains more than a thousand exercises, wide-ranging and often difficult.<ref name=memoir>{{cite book |title=Jacob Theodore Schwartz: A Biographical Memoir |last1=Davis |first1=Martin |last2=Schonberg |first2=Edmond |date=2011 |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/schwartz-jacob-t.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802174935/https://www.nasonline.org/publications/biographical-memoirs/memoir-pdfs/schwartz-jacob-t.pdf |archive-date=2 August 2022 |access-date=3 July 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{rp|5}} One particularly difficult exercise was not solved until Dunford assigned it to a young [[Robert Langlands]].<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|37}}{{efn|The second volume contains a thanks to Langlands, noting that "R. Langlands has shown that Exercise III.9.20 [in volume one] is false and as a result has made a decided improvement on a result of [[Pavel Alexandrov|Alexandroff]] (III.5.13)."<ref>Dunford, Nelson; Schwartz, Jacob T. (1988). ''Linear Operators''. Vol. 2. Wiley-Interscience.</ref>{{rp|vi}} Rota recalled that, when called attention to this exercise, nobody could recall how it had made its way into the book and neither Dunford nor Schwartz could not solve it. Dunford happened to assign it to Langlands when he took Dunford's course.<ref name=Rota/>{{rp|37}} According to Langlands' recollection, "One exercise in their collection had to be corrected, but it took some effort to convince Dunford of this and some time before he was willing to listen to my explanations and, I suppose, examine my counter-example."<ref>{{cite book |last=Langlands |first=Robert P. |title=Interview with Farzin Barekat for the University of British Columbia |date=2009 |url=https://publications.ias.edu/sites/default/files/interview-ubc-2009-rpl.pdf |access-date=13 June 2024 }}</ref>{{rp|12}}}}
